items.title: Jim H. Dunbar Jr. Interview, 1959-11-28
items.q: if it is Beryl House or however Danny Barker described it

ctx.x: Well, you know, the thing that really gets me about that band, it's a brass band and the other brass bands have air monitors. But it's like Danny Ruffer said about it. If somebody ever recorded that barrel house brass band and it is really barrel house. Now they can sit there and read those directors and play them pretty straight. You know, you've heard that, about it. No deal. Mm-hmm. But God, they can't really get down to the line, you know. See, it's exciting. Yeah.

Well, you know, I think a white person, we've discussed this many times, but we've discussed the merits, as many people have, of white and Negro musicians. Whether there's any point in discussing that or not, it's not the point here. The point is that one thing certain, I think, about any Negro musician is that he certainly knows legitimacy in a jazz band. This is not the discussion of a degree of musicianship or anything of that sort, but if a band has got it, if it breathes as far, and if it swings, if it is…

Well, you know, something that I've really noticed, maybe this is unique to New Orleans, maybe it's just human being, but, it's a band that goes down the street. Just can't help but notice people who come out on their galleries, you know, and it can be anybody. It could be any section of town, any class of people you want to name.
